text.p: President Bill Clinton is passionately defending his right to discuss foreign policy and other issues with political donors -- insisting "that's the way the democratic system works."

Clinton, in Florida to participate in a two-day golf tourney hosted by golfing legend Greg Norman that begins on Friday, Thursday night told a political fund-raising dinner that generated $1 million that there was nothing wrong with his hearing their thoughts on issues facing the nation -- particularly on the international front.

Since his successful re-election in November, Clinton and his fellow Democrats have been caught in a swirl of controversy over fund-raising tactics and suggestions that some of the donations bought access to lobby the president or his staff.
Gazing out at his audience of well-dressed donors, Clinton declared: "I don't know how many of you tonight came up to me and had detailed conversations with me about the Middle East peace process.

"I think it's a good thing that you can talk to your president about the Middle East peace process," Clinton said, noting that on Monday, he expected to discuss the situation in Northern Ireland with guests invited to the White House for St. Patrick Day celebrations.

"And I might say, I think it's a good thing that my supporters feel free to talk to me about issues relating to their relationships with Cuba, with the Middle East, with Northern Ireland, with the Everglads or anything else you've got on your mind," Clinton said.

"That's the way the democratic system works, and I'm proud you're here and glad you talked to me about these things," the president said to the applause of the crowd made up of individuals who had each paid $5,000 to be in the room.

Clinton's comments follow months of unfolding discoveries about the frenzy of Democratic activists to raise cash for the presidental election, and suggestions some may have come illegally from foreign sources. The party has been forced to announce it will return some $3 million in donations because of suspicious sources for the contributions.
His remarks in praise of campaign contributors and their right to talk to him about their concerns amounted to a rebuttal of critics who have raised questions about influence peddling.

Republicans have been calling for Attorney General Janet Reno to appoint an independent counsel to investigate Democratic fund-raising practices during the past campaign, but she says no evidence has been found to warrent such a probe.

Clinton has been trying be on both sides of the issue -- often railing against those who stand in the way of campaign finance reforms he says are badly needed, and hours later going to a political fund-raiser that he says should be outlawed.
The president insists that he is only playing by the rules as they currently exist, even though he sees the flaws of the system, because that is what Republican rivals do.
